title: The AI Trade, Rising Rates, and Why the Market Is Still Standing - The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 73

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/The AI Trade, Rising Rates, and Why the Market Is Still Standing - The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 73.docx

summary: Eisman interviews Strategas strategists in Aug 2026 on the AI trade, rising rates and why equities hold up. They see a strong economy, rotational tape, internals improving, and an equity-ending 10-year yield level far above 4.5%.

coverage.note: intro, Situational Awareness blowup, market concentration, macro risk list
levered long/short trap, LTCM analogy, breadth, rate threshold for equities, bubble-year yield analogies
rising yields with rising stocks, PMIs, tax expensing, Warsh Fed communication regime, QE distribution
E not P/E, alpha market, asset managers, private equity illiquidity
oil and war, base metals vs iron ore, hyperscaler financing
hyperscaler cash flow and capital intensity; sponsor reads (Longangle, Qwoka) excluded
Google equity raise, semis vs hyperscalers, sentiment swing, OpenAI/Anthropic concentration
AI-adjacent names, Meta earnings, expense growth and depreciation
litigation as punishment, lobbying, global banks, deregulation
private credit, bank curve view, Europe vs Japan; DripDrop sponsor read excluded
staples, health care, populism, 10-year range, Fed guidance complaints
volatility ahead, Eisman takeaway on 4.5% threshold

completeness_estimate: 0.85 - the first reader captured nearly all the main market claims, numbers and analogies (about 80 claims); added points are secondary reasoning (nominal-growth framing of the yield threshold, Fed regime intent, Japan vs Europe supporting evidence, litigation and policy risks); no clear misstatements found

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: if you look at the top 10 holdings of the S&P 500, I think that's 39%. If you look at the tech sector, I think it's 36%.
claims.claim: The S&P 500 is highly concentrated (top 10 about 39%, tech about 36%, over 50% with tech-adjacent names), so index risk depends on a few AI-linked stocks.
claims.indicator: S&P 500 top-10 weight / tech sector weight

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: that happened with the VIX below 20 and and a modest increase in interest rates, you know, to 15, 20 basis point increase in long-term interest rates
claims.claim: A large hedge fund (Situational Awareness) blew up with VIX under 20 and only a 15-20 bp rise in long yields, showing leveraged thematic books can fail in quiet markets.
claims.conditions: low VIX and small rate move did not protect a levered thematic book
claims.testable: partly - blow-up events are rare and hard to define

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: Fed, of course, which is the other big war is really the big issue.
claims.claim: The macro risks named are the war and oil, tariffs returning, hyperscaler capex debate and the Fed, which together make forward progress hard for the market.

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: But if you're four times levered [laughter] and let's imagine there's a bad auto accident.
claims.claim: A trade can be right on the long-run theme but wipe out a levered fund if long and short legs are the same bet and it reverses short term.
claims.conditions: leverage (here 4x) with long and short legs correlated to one theme
claims.testable: partly - can test drawdowns of theme-neutral vs levered pairs

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: So, listen, and it's I don't know, it reminds me of Long-Term Capital a bit, of course.
claims.claim: The Situational Awareness failure resembles LTCM: a famous, confident, levered fund undone by a single correlated bet.

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: You only had about 50% of the S&P above the 200-day average on June 2nd. Today, we sit here today with 75% of the S&P above uh the 200-day.
claims.claim: Market internals (share of S&P above its 200-day average) improved from 50% to 75% even as leaders corrected 30-50%, so the market is rotating not breaking.

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: until we find what level of interest rate is truly competitive to equities, you're going to stay in this highly rotational tape.
claims.claim: Money stays in equities and rotates between sectors until the risk-free rate gets high enough to compete with stocks.
claims.indicator: long-term Treasury yield level vs equities
claims.conditions: until yields reach a level that competes with equities

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: We we thought it was 450. That's what I thought. Because in in 24, you know, 23, 24, 25, it was for it was largely 450, right?
claims.claim: The 10-year yield level that triggered equity corrections in 2023-25 was about 4.5%, but the threshold now looks higher.
claims.indicator: US 10-year yield about 4.5% as equity pain threshold
claims.conditions: threshold has drifted up with nominal growth near 6.5%
claims.testable: partly - threshold can be backtested but is unstable

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: look at some of the great bubble-like environments, whether it was Japan in '89, JGB yields went four to eight that year as the Nikkei was melting up, or Nasdaq in '99, US 10s went four to seven that year.
claims.claim: In past bubbles (Japan 1989, Nasdaq 1999) long yields rose sharply while equities kept rising, so the rate level that ends a cycle is far higher than people expect.
claims.indicator: 10-year government bond yields during equity bubbles
claims.direction: equities keep rising while yields rise, until a much higher level

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: '87, right? They went from six to nine long rates went from six to nine percent while the stock market was up 30%.
claims.claim: In 1987 long rates rose from 6% to 9% while stocks were up 30% before the crash, another case of rising yields not ending an equity run quickly.

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: that's kind of the worst sign when when stocks are going straight up, and they don't care at the same time long-term interest rates are going up, and the stock market seems impervious.
claims.claim: Stocks rising while long yields rise and the market ignores it is the point of greatest risk, a late-cycle warning.
claims.indicator: equity trend vs long-term yield trend
claims.direction: raises risk of eventual equity decline
claims.testable: yes - can test joint condition of equity up and yield up

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: I think the PMIs show you that um there's mar- the economy is still expanding and actually pretty rapidly.
claims.claim: PMIs indicate the economy is still expanding rapidly, supporting the view that the economy is strong.

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: Because you get to write off the entire amount.
claims.claim: The one big beautiful bill allows full expensing of capital investment, an incentive for capex across all US companies, not only hyperscalers.

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: It may wind up being they have to tighten because of growth. And I think that's a very different message than second half '21 into '22.
claims.claim: A Fed that tightens because of strong growth rather than inflation is a different, less equity-hostile regime than 2022.

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: The backup in interest rates has largely been in real rates. It hasn't been in inflation, right?
claims.claim: The recent rise in yields is in real rates rather than inflation breakevens, which argues against Fed tightening.

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: So Warsh's view, which I agree with, is that it's been too big a free pass for the financial markets and capital to basically just take as much risk as they can.
claims.claim: Detailed Fed communication (statements since 1994, press conferences since 2019) removes risk and encourages speculation, so cutting forward guidance should raise volatility and cut risk-taking.
claims.direction: less guidance -> higher volatility, less speculation
claims.conditions: new Fed chair Warsh reducing communication

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: last week Warsh said the reaction function when you're at full employment is inflation.
claims.claim: At full employment the Fed's reaction function is inflation, so the Fed will respond to inflation prints rather than growth.
claims.indicator: Fed reaction function at full employment
claims.testable: partly - reaction function can be fitted

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: QE was much better for Wall Street than it was and wealthy people than it was for the average person.
claims.claim: QE and near-zero rates benefited asset holders far more than ordinary savers, who held savings accounts earning zero.
claims.direction: asset prices up, savers' income down

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: if you look at 2026, it's been about the E, not the P/E.
claims.claim: In 2026 the market is driven by earnings growth rather than multiple expansion: P/E is down two or three turns, which marks a more cyclical, earnings-dependent regime.
claims.testable: yes - decompose returns into E and P/E

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: This is a market where I think stock picking and active uh matters a lot more than passive.
claims.claim: The strategists call this an alpha market where stock picking and active management matter more than passive, citing asset-manager stocks breaking out.
claims.indicator: relative performance of active asset managers (State Street, T. Rowe, Invesco)
claims.direction: active over passive; asset-manager stocks outperform
claims.testable: partly - dispersion and active share can be tested

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: in private equity, the monetization time frame is now like 7 years.
claims.claim: Private equity exits now take about 7 years, so institutions that chose PE for low reported volatility are illiquid and must cut spending (colleges, with Notre Dame at about 50% PE and venture).

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: So, you're going to have a bid in the price of oil, um which is the main uh issue.
claims.claim: Oil supply disruptions will persist whether or not the war ends, so oil keeps a bid despite peace headlines.

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: There's a lot more reflexivity to higher oil prices in Europe where they don't have this AI capex story underway.
claims.claim: Higher oil matters more for equities in regions without an AI capex impulse (Europe), while in the US capex dominates the war and oil effect.
claims.indicator: oil price sensitivity of regional equity markets

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: The move Franklin crude was pretty tepid.
claims.claim: Crude's rebound after renewed fighting was tepid, only reaching the high 90s and back under 80, so the oil risk premium for war headlines is fading.
claims.indicator: crude oil price reaction to war headlines

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: there actually is an oversupply of oil. That that China has completely withdrawn from purchasing oil and so that demand is much much lower than people think.
claims.claim: A guest argues oil is in oversupply because China has pulled back purchases and bypass pipelines for the strait are nearly built.

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: copper new high, zinc new high, tin new high, Chinese iron ore is collapsing right here.
claims.claim: Base metals at new highs alongside collapsing iron ore indicate metals strength is from AI and capex demand, not China.
claims.indicator: copper, zinc, tin vs iron ore
claims.direction: base metals up on AI capex; China demand weak

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: Um it's going to be hard to continue to grow AI investments without further dilution of shareholders. Mainly cuz you saw Google issue 85 billion dollars in equity and the all the hyperscalers are issuing debt now.
claims.claim: Hyperscaler AI capex now needs external financing (Google $85bn equity, debt issuance, Oracle downgrade), so growth in AI investment implies shareholder dilution.

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: the cash flow of the hyperscalers over the next couple of years looks like it's going to be negative.
claims.claim: Hyperscaler free cash flow is falling or negative (Meta $785m for the quarter, Microsoft about $19bn and down 25%, Amazon negative over 12 months).

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: One thing that is not arguable is that the what's not arguable is that the business has become incredibly capital intensive.
claims.claim: Big tech has moved from asset-light cash-flow machines to capital-intensive businesses, which changes how it should be valued.

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: I don't see how you do it without hitting the bond and and equity markets, right?
claims.claim: The AI capex plans cannot be funded from internal cash flow and will require bond and equity issuance.
claims.direction: more supply of equity and debt

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: last time they actually raised equity capital was in the 2000s.
claims.claim: Google raising $85bn of equity, its first raise since the early 2000s, marks a regime shift in big-tech funding.

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: I'm actually a little more bullish, believe it or not, on the semiconductors in a way because I I do think the hyperscalers are going to continue to spend money
claims.claim: Demand for AI exceeds supply so chip suppliers benefit from hyperscaler capex, while hyperscaler returns on that spend are uncertain and may be competed away.
claims.direction: long semiconductors over hyperscalers; market-weight tech

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: the attitudes towards some of the hyperscalers kind of reached a fever pitch of negativity maybe two or three weeks ago
claims.claim: Sentiment on hyperscalers swung from extreme negativity to sharp rebounds (Microsoft's best 5-day move since 1987 IPO, Amazon new highs), so sentiment-driven rotation is tradeable at the sector level.
claims.testable: partly - sentiment extremes can be proxied by drawdown

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: I think that's been mistaken for some deterioration in AI fundamentals when it's just been we have to think about them a little bit differently.
claims.claim: Investors mistook the need for a new valuation framework for big tech (capital intensive, not cash-flow machines) for deteriorating AI fundamentals.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: something like 70% of the AI hyperscaler revenue is from just those two companies.
claims.claim: About 70% of AI hyperscaler revenue comes from OpenAI and Anthropic, both with negative cash flow, so trouble at either would hit the whole AI ecosystem.
claims.direction: negative AI ecosystem if the two fail

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: The one big beautiful bill is really a bet on productivity to bail you out of inflation.
claims.claim: The fiscal expansion and AI capex are together a bet that productivity growth will offset inflation.

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: So, I I think you kind of have to give these the benefit of the doubt on until they you know, attempt to rally, don't make new highs, and fail. And we haven't seen that yet.
claims.claim: A leadership group is not finished after a 30% correction until it rallies, fails to make new highs and rolls over; AI-adjacent build-out names (Quanta, Caterpillar) have rebounded strongly.
claims.indicator: AI build-out stocks, new-high tests after corrections

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: in 20 late 2022 it was the stock that got Zuckerberg to change course.
claims.claim: A 50-60% drawdown in Meta in 2022 was the market signal that forced management to cut metaverse spending, and the stock bottomed near $90.
claims.indicator: stock price as discipline on management capex

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: the velocity with which Meta reversed the earnings decline in the last week it is pretty notable.
claims.claim: Meta fully recovered a 10-12% post-earnings drop within three days; a fast reversal of an earnings gap-down is respected as a chart signal.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: the revenue grew 28% which is powerful and the expenses grew 55%
claims.claim: Meta's revenue grew 28% but expenses grew 55%, with depreciation rising from $4bn to $6bn and heading to $12bn, which will weigh on earnings.
claims.indicator: Meta expense growth vs revenue growth; depreciation

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: the lawsuit was the punishment
claims.claim: Long antitrust cases distract management even if the company wins (IBM in the 1970s missed personal computing; Microsoft in the 1990s), so legal overhang is a drag on big tech.
claims.indicator: litigation exposure of big tech (Meta social media suits)
claims.direction: negative for companies in prolonged litigation

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: the lobbying stuff is very important. It can be an alpha generator.
claims.claim: Lobbying and Washington relations can generate alpha because government increasingly shapes the AI industry.

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: Japanese banks continue to lead. European banks have been absolutely exceptional throughout all of this
claims.claim: Banks globally (US, Japanese, European, brokers) are leaders, and the private credit scare did not become a systemic banking threat; double-B spreads hit new cycle lows.
claims.testable: yes - bank index and spread data

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: we are in a extreme period of financial deregulation um and really you can't really shrink the balance sheet of the Fed until you deregulate the the banks the banks.
claims.claim: Deregulation of banks is a precondition for shrinking the Fed balance sheet and supports bank stocks.

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: I just can't think of too many times in my career or historically where you're on the verge of a big problem and every bank stock around the world is at new highs.
claims.claim: Bank stocks worldwide at new highs is a signal that no major credit problem is imminent, since banks usually lead on trouble.
claims.indicator: global bank stock index at new highs
claims.testable: yes - bank index new highs vs later drawdowns

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: I think private credit was largely a regulatory arb.
claims.claim: Private credit grew because post-crisis regulation (Dodd-Frank) pushed banks out of lending, so private credit is a regulatory arbitrage that could be disproportionately bad for wealthy holders in a downturn but is not systemic.

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: First of all, I think the curve is going to steepen.
claims.claim: Banks should benefit from a steeper yield curve and minimal credit losses because the economy is strong.
claims.indicator: yield curve slope; bank credit losses

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: The reason why it's cheap is that they're not dynamic economies.
claims.claim: European equities are cheap for a reason: low-dynamism economies without AI, so cheapness alone is not a buy signal.
claims.testable: partly - value vs growth in region

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: Personally, I like Japan a lot better um as an investment, and I'm invested there.
claims.claim: Japan is preferred over Europe because it is exiting deflation and has a return-on-equity reform (delisting firms below price-to-book and ROE minimums).

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: believe it or not the Euro Stoxx is at a new high right now as we speak, but it's it's much uh more focused into a few groups or names.
claims.claim: European index highs are narrow: AI build-out names (Schneider, Siemens Energy) plus banks, while autos and luxury, which depend on Chinese demand, are in multi-year bear markets.
claims.indicator: Euro Stoxx; auto and luxury sectors

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: higher higher JGB yields I think entirely reflect this reflationary animal that's been unleashed there.
claims.claim: Higher JGB yields reflect reflation not distress and are good for Japanese equities (yields fell for 30-40 years without helping them); the warning would be weakness in Japanese banks and insurers.
claims.indicator: JGB yields; Japanese bank and insurance stocks
claims.conditions: bank and insurer stocks stay strong
claims.testable: yes - JGB yield and bank stock series

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: Japanese 10-year yields are about to cross German 10-year yields for the first time in decades?
claims.claim: Japanese 10-year yields are about to exceed German 10-year yields for the first time in decades.

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: Regulated utilities have traded poorly all year.
claims.claim: Regulated utilities have been weak and making new lows, and unregulated power producers are weakening too, which the speaker attributes to politics consuming the sector.

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: Kraft Heinz, Hershey's all starting to bottom here.
claims.claim: Consumer staples may be forming bottoms after two bad years (Kraft Heinz, Hershey) but remain the weakest defensive sector.

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: So if I'm going to rate kind of defensives, health care comes at the top of that pile.
claims.claim: Healthcare ranks first among defensives: pharma, biotech and life sciences (Thermo, Danaher, Illumina) are leading and made major bottoms, and health insurers put in lows.

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: there is a reaction against big anything. Big big media, big academia, big pharma, big banks
claims.claim: Increasingly populist politics produces a reaction against large institutions, creating policy risk for large pharma, banks, oil and others.

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: this is the narrowest range in 10-year yields that we've ever seen. The range of the 10 years 85 basis points over the last 400 days.
claims.claim: The 10-year yield range of 85 bp over 400 days since inauguration is the narrowest ever, so the yield move is not yet explosive enough to disrupt equities.

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: I want to be spoon-fed.
claims.claim: Market participants complaining about less Fed forward guidance (media, hedge funds) have a self-interest in guidance and the complaints are overstated.

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: Good companies will still get rewarded.
claims.claim: With the Fed no longer sowing certainty, markets will see higher volatility while good companies are still rewarded.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: they thought that if the 10-year got above 4.5% that would really put a kibosh on the stock market because bonds would be much more appealing.
claims.claim: Eisman's summary: strategists expected a 4.5% 10-year to hurt stocks but it did not, so they now say the 10-year must go significantly higher before a correction, and they stay bullish unless that or an AI collapse happens.
claims.conditions: 10y not significantly higher and AI story intact

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: I don't think 10s are going to seven here, but with nominal at six and a half, um maybe it's a level higher than people think
claims.claim: The 10-year yield that would end the equity cycle should be judged against nominal growth: with nominal GDP growth near 6.5%, the threshold is higher than the old 4.5%, though not as extreme as 7% as in 1999.
claims.direction: equities tolerate higher yields while nominal growth is high
claims.testable: yes - yield minus nominal growth vs subsequent equity returns

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: If I told you the leading stocks, Cisco or Sun Micro, were going to be down 40 or 50% over an 8-week period, what do you think the S&P or the Nasdaq would be down
claims.claim: In 1999-2000 a 40-50% fall in the leading stocks in eight weeks would have dragged the index down a lot; that the index withstood a similar fall in semis and hyperscalers in 2026 is evidence of unusual internal strength.
claims.testable: yes - index vs leader drawdowns across episodes

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: We're trying to make Fed monetary policy that fits the entire economy, not just what he believes, I believe, that is very much skewed towards Wall Street
claims.claim: The new Fed leadership intends to end the 15-16 years of near-zero rates that favored financial markets and to set policy for the whole economy, so the Fed will be less supportive of asset prices and markets must adjust.
claims.direction: less policy support for asset prices

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: I can't think of an industry that benefited more from near zero percent interest rates than private equity
claims.claim: Private equity was the main beneficiary of near-zero rates, so it is the part of the financial system most exposed to a higher-rate regime (slow exits, trapped capital).
claims.direction: private equity stress when rates stay high

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: it's a tennis match, right? It's one day it's on, one day it's off
claims.claim: War and peace headlines whipsaw the market with no discernible rhyme or reason, so there is little tradeable edge in headline timing; the durable factor is the oil supply disruption.

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: Yes. And their willingness or they or propensity to try to slow it down in some way
claims.claim: Washington's propensity to slow AI through regulation (with New York cited, comparable to what was done to fracking) is a policy risk for the AI build-out, which is why big tech invests in government relations.

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: Meta has a lot of lawsuits, all these social media, you know, lawsuits by people who are claiming of claiming that the algorithms are basically making them mentally ill
claims.claim: Hundreds of social-media harm lawsuits (two already lost by Meta) add legal overhang and a possible earnings drag; individually small versus revenue, they accumulate.
claims.indicator: social media litigation count and losses
claims.conditions: verdicts continue to go against the company

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: Japan has so many more of the themes that the market has craved, uh whether it's chips, whether it's AI buildout, um you know, a a bigger defense industry
claims.claim: Japan outperforms Europe in part because its sector mix has the themes the market wants (chips, AI build-out, defense), while Europe's index highs rest on a few AI-build-out names and banks.
claims.conditions: AI capex and defense themes persist

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: German GDP basically has not grown for the last like four five years, not a dollar
claims.claim: German GDP has not grown for four to five years, supporting the view that Europe's cheap valuations reflect an absence of growth dynamism.

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: the richest families in Europe are largely the same richest families in Europe from 400 years ago
claims.claim: Studies show Europe's richest families are largely the same as 400 years ago while the US has high wealth turnover (shirt sleeves to shirt sleeves in three generations), a structural reason Europe is less dynamic and a harder place to make money.

claims.speaker: Chris Verrone
claims.quote: I got too dogmatic on those and I missed it
claims.claim: The strategist admits being too dogmatic about health insurers (UNH, Cigna) and missing the major lows in late 2025 to early 2026, a reminder to let the chart override a fixed group view.

claims.speaker: Jason Trennert
claims.quote: the expansion in the role of government actually is working worked for them for many years
claims.claim: Health care benefited for years from the expanding role of government, but pricing pressure now runs the other way (any pricing action reduces revenue), a policy headwind despite the chart strength.
claims.direction: policy risk for health care pricing

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: the big issue is whether all this money being spent on AI is going to prove to be good, but we won't know that for a while
claims.claim: Whether AI capex pays off will not be known for a long time, so the AI-collapse risk is a slow-resolving background risk, while the near-term trigger to watch is the 10-year yield moving significantly above its prior ceiling.
claims.direction: bullish unless yields surge or AI story breaks
